title: AshML — Training curves
description: Losses, accuracies and learning rates on the step axis the runs reported them against, read from `training_metrics` over the PostgreSQL datasource (ADR 0009).

list.name: project
list.label: Project
list.query:
SELECT DISTINCT p.name
  FROM projects p
  JOIN training_jobs j ON j.project_id = p.id
  JOIN training_metrics m ON m.job_id = j.id
 ORDER BY 1
list.description: Only projects that have reported at least one metric. A project with no runs would offer an empty job list and a blank dashboard.

list.name: job
list.label: Run
list.query:
SELECT j.name || ' · ' || left(j.id::text, 8) AS __text,
       j.id::text                                 AS __value
  FROM training_jobs j
  JOIN projects p ON p.id = j.project_id
 WHERE p.name = '$project'
   AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM training_metrics m WHERE m.job_id = j.id)
 ORDER BY j.created_at DESC
list.description: The short id is in the label because run names repeat — every chaos script names its job after itself — and a curve attributed to the wrong run is worse than no curve.

list.name: metric
list.label: Any other metric
list.query:
SELECT DISTINCT name
  FROM training_metrics
 WHERE job_id::text IN (${job:sqlstring})
 ORDER BY 1
list.description: The metric names are whatever the training script chose to log — this schema stores them long, one row per name, so nothing here needs a migration when a run logs something new.

options.content:
### These curves do not come from Prometheus, and that is the design

A loss belongs to a **step**, and only the training loop knows which one. A scraper sampling on a timer would record *"loss was 1.84 at 14:03:22"* — the wrong axis — and would silently drop every step between two scrapes. So runs **push** their metrics (ADR 0009), `training_metrics` keeps the step the run reported, and these panels read it directly over the PostgreSQL datasource. The x-axis below is steps, not time, which is why these are Trend panels rather than time series.

The cost is stated plainly: a training script that does not call the SDK reports nothing, and AshML will not invent a curve for it.

**A resumed run may report the same step twice.** Those steps were genuinely trained twice — the retry restarts from the last confirmed checkpoint — and the points are drawn as they were reported rather than averaged into one line that never happened.

panels.title: Runs in view
panels.description: `attempt` above zero means this run was retried and resumed from a checkpoint. `first_report` is when the *training process* observed the first point, not when the API received it — a run that buffers and flushes in a batch would otherwise have its whole history collapse onto the moment of the flush.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT j.name                                        AS run,
       left(j.id::text, 8)                          AS id,
       j.state                                      AS state,
       j.attempt                                    AS attempt,
       max(m.step)                                  AS last_step,
       count(DISTINCT m.name)                       AS metrics,
       count(*)                                     AS points,
       min(m.recorded_at)                           AS first_report,
       max(m.recorded_at)                           AS last_report
  FROM training_jobs j
  JOIN training_metrics m ON m.job_id = j.id
 WHERE j.id::text IN (${job:sqlstring})
 GROUP BY 1, 2, 3, 4
 ORDER BY min(m.recorded_at) DESC

panels.title: Loss, against step
panels.description: Training loss and, where the run reported one, validation loss. A discontinuity here on a resumed run is the thing worth looking at: weights, optimizer moments *and* the learning-rate schedule are restored on resume, and restoring the first two without the third produces a run that trains, converges and looks healthy while following a different curve from the one its experiment record claims.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT m.step                                                    AS step,
       j.name || ' · ' || left(j.id::text, 8) || ' · ' || m.name AS series,
       m.value                                                   AS value
  FROM training_metrics m
  JOIN training_jobs j ON j.id = m.job_id
 WHERE j.id::text IN (${job:sqlstring})
   AND m.name IN ('loss', 'val_loss')
 ORDER BY series, m.step, m.recorded_at

panels.title: Accuracy, against step
panels.description: Whatever the run called it. The ResNet-18 run recorded here reached 65.59% top-1 on the full 10 000-image CIFAR-10 test set after one epoch — which is undertrained and should never be quoted as a CIFAR-10 result. It is here to show the platform carried a real workload, not to say anything about ResNet-18.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT m.step                                                    AS step,
       j.name || ' · ' || left(j.id::text, 8) || ' · ' || m.name AS series,
       m.value                                                   AS value
  FROM training_metrics m
  JOIN training_jobs j ON j.id = m.job_id
 WHERE j.id::text IN (${job:sqlstring})
   AND m.name IN ('accuracy', 'train_accuracy', 'val_accuracy')
 ORDER BY series, m.step, m.recorded_at

panels.title: Learning rate, against step
panels.description: The series that proves a resume actually resumed. A OneCycle schedule restored correctly shows one curve across the kill; a schedule that restarted repeats its opening value at the step the checkpoint was taken. That is the check `make chaos-resume-resnet` makes, and this is where you can see it.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT m.step                                                    AS step,
       j.name || ' · ' || left(j.id::text, 8) || ' · ' || m.name AS series,
       m.value                                                   AS value
  FROM training_metrics m
  JOIN training_jobs j ON j.id = m.job_id
 WHERE j.id::text IN (${job:sqlstring})
   AND m.name IN ('lr')
 ORDER BY series, m.step, m.recorded_at

panels.title: $metric, against step
panels.description: For whatever else a run logged — `steps_per_second` on the workloads here. The set of metric names belongs to the training script, not to this schema, so this panel follows it rather than needing a new panel each time.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT m.step                                                    AS step,
       j.name || ' · ' || left(j.id::text, 8) || ' · ' || m.name AS series,
       m.value                                                   AS value
  FROM training_metrics m
  JOIN training_jobs j ON j.id = m.job_id
 WHERE j.id::text IN (${job:sqlstring})
   AND m.name IN ('$metric')
 ORDER BY series, m.step, m.recorded_at

panels.title: Last reported value of every metric
panels.description: The *last* value, not the best one. A best-value column invites reporting the high-water mark of a run that then diverged, and the number a model version carries is the one measured on the artifact that was registered.

targets.rawSql:
SELECT DISTINCT ON (j.id, m.name)
       j.name              AS run,
       left(j.id::text, 8) AS id,
       m.name              AS metric,
       m.value             AS last_value,
       m.step              AS at_step,
       m.recorded_at       AS recorded_at
  FROM training_metrics m
  JOIN training_jobs j ON j.id = m.job_id
 WHERE j.id::text IN (${job:sqlstring})
 ORDER BY j.id, m.name, m.step DESC, m.recorded_at DESC
